paragraphs.text: Lesson 18, childhood.
Nora and Jolene are chatting about their experiences as children.
Listen to their conversation and choose the best answer for each question.
I was so clumsy when I was a kid.
There was this one time my family went to the circus and I remember tumbling down three flights of stairs,
crashing into the popcorn cellar and finally colliding with the girl eating ice cream.
Yikes, I was pretty uncoordinated too.
Did you ever mistake strangers for your parents?
No, did you?
A bunch of times.
Once I was in the grocery store and my mom was busy rearranging the food in our cart,
I saw this dark haired man leaning into a freezer to grab some frozen meals.
He looked just like my dad from the back.
So I ran up to him, hugged him and said,
Hi dad!
When he turned around, both of us were startled.
I can imagine.
Did you ever stay up past your bedtime when you were a kid?
You bet.
I would turn off my lights and go under my bed sheets with a flashlight to read or do coloring books.
Sometimes me and my two brothers would sneak out of our rooms and play hide and seek in the dark.
We'd have to wait till about midnight to be sure my parents were sound asleep.
Sounds like fun, but did you ever get in trouble?
Yeah, one time when I dozed off while hiding in a closet,
my brothers couldn't find me so they gave up and went to bed.
Then in the morning, my mom saw I wasn't in my room and she flipped out.
Oh, that's funny.
Well, not so much for your mom at the time, but I'm sure she was glad you were all right.
Of course she was, but we still got punished.
All three of us were grounded for a week, and we had to do extra chores.
I usually managed to weasel out of getting punished.
My mom was pretty strict, but my dad was a total pushover.
Every time I pleaded with him to let me off the hook, he'd eventually give in.
I used to drive my mom up the wall.
That definitely wouldn't fly with my parents.
When it came to decisions involving us kids, they backed each other up.
Sometimes I wish I could turn back the clock and be a kid again.
I used to roam around the neighborhood without a care in the world.
Not me.
After picking me up from school, my mom would drag me along on all her errands.
Bummer.
What about during the summers?
Did you ever go to summer camp?
Every year.
I think my parents sent us to camp just to get us out of their hair, but it was awesome.
We got to do stuff like horseback riding, canoeing, having water balloon fights, the whole nine yards.
Those were the days, that's for sure.
Let's learn the vocabulary from this conversation about childhood.
Nora says that she was so clumsy when she was a kid.
The word clumsy describes a person who is not graceful, not physically coordinated.
A clumsy person is always having small accidents.
When Nora went to the circus, she remembers tumbling down three flights of stairs.
Tumbling down means falling in a disorganized way.
And the expression flights of stairs refers to the fact that each section of stairs going from one floor to another is called a flight.
Jolene reacts by saying, yikes.
The exclamation, yikes, is an expression of surprise or mild shock.
Jolene asks Nora if she's ever mistaken strangers for her parents.
Jolene says she's done it a bunch of times.
A bunch of means several or many.
When Jolene was in the supermarket with her mom, she saw a dark-haired man leaning into a freezer.
The word leaning means he was inclining his body.
She thought this man was her father, so she hugged him and said,
Hi Dad!
But when he turned around, both of us were startled.
The word startled means mildly frightened or shocked.
Nora then asks, did you ever stay up past your bedtime when you were a kid?
The phrasal verb stay up, in this case means remain awake.
And Jolene says, you bet.
You bet means definitely.
Nora describes how she and her two brothers would sneak out of their rooms.
To sneak out means to go out in a quiet or secret way without anybody else noticing.
Nora and her brothers would play hide and seek in the dark.
Hide and seek is a game played by children where some children hide and one child looks for the people who are hiding.
To play this game, Nora and her brothers had to wait until about midnight to be sure their parents were sound asleep.
Sound asleep means sleeping deeply and not likely to wake up.
To describe this state, we can say, sound asleep or fast asleep.
However, Nora got into some trouble when she dozed off while hiding in a closet.
The phrasal verb, dozed off means she fell asleep.
Her brothers couldn't find her, so they gave up and went to bed.
Gave up means they stopped, they desisted.
Then, in the morning, Nora's mom saw that she wasn't in her room, and she flipped out.
She flipped out means she became very upset and agitated.
This is a slang or informal expression.
Jolene points out that Nora's mother was probably glad that Nora was all right.
The word glad is another word for happy.
Nora says she was, but there was still a punishment.
All three of the kids were grounded for a week.
The word grounded refers to a punishment where kids or teenagers are not allowed to leave the house to meet their friends or do fun things.
They can only go to school and stay at home.
Another part of the punishment was that Nora and her brothers had to do extra chores.
The word chores means obligatory tasks, especially housework, like cleaning or taking out the garbage.
Jolene usually managed to weasel out of getting punished.
Weasel out of means to escape an obligation in a deceptive way.
The reason was that Jolene's dad was a total pushover.
A pushover is a person who is easily persuaded.
It's easy to make or convince this person to change their mind.
Jolene pleaded with her father not to punish her.
Pleated with means asked with a lot of emotion.
And eventually her father would give in.
Give in means to stop resisting and agree to do what someone else wants you to do.
Jolene says this tendency of her father used to drive her mom up the wall.
To drive somebody up the wall means to make that person extremely annoyed.
Other expressions for this are drive someone crazy or drive someone nuts.
Nora says that strategy definitely wouldn't fly with her parents.
Wouldn't fly is an informal way to say it wouldn't work.
It wouldn't have any results.
When it came to decisions involving the kids, Nora's parents backed each other up.
In this context, backed each other up means they supported each other.
Jolene wishes she could turn back the clock and be a kid again.
To turn back the clock means to go back to how things were in the past.
Jolene used to roam around the neighborhood without a care in the world.
To roam around means to move around a large area without any particular direction.
And the phrase without a care in the world means she was completely free of worries.
Nora's experience was different.
After her mom picked her up from school, she would drag Nora along on all her errands.
To drag someone along means to take that person when they weren't willing to go.
And errands are short trips to perform specific tasks for daily life,
like going to the supermarket, bank, post office, etc.
We usually use the verb run with errands.
For example, I'm going to run some errands.
Jolene responds, bummer.
The word bummer is a slang way to say that's unpleasant or unfortunate.
And then she asks Nora about summer camp.
Nora used to go to summer camp every year.
She says, I think my parents sent us to camp just to get us out of their hair.
This phrase, get us out of their hair means make us go away so we would stop bothering them.
Nora describes summer camp as awesome.
She did activities like horseback riding, canoeing, having water balloon fights, the whole nine yards.
The whole nine yards means and everything that's included in that experience.
Jolene comments, those were the days, that's for sure.
The expression, those were the days, means that was a good time in the past.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
Go ahead and try the vocabulary quiz to put these expressions into practice and the speaking
task to get some feedback on your spoken English.
